CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Choir — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the choir club habit: breathe together first, sing rounds second, and end with a two-part song where the family genuinely becomes a choir.

What is this?

Choir club is group singing with listening at the center — unison songs, rounds, and simple two-part harmonies. The card’s printed skills are Voice & Harmony: your own sound and the art of fitting it to everyone else’s.

What does it mean?

Singing in a group trains the ear more than the throat: holding your part while another part moves is advanced listening. Rounds (the same song, started at different times) teach harmony without needing to teach harmony.

What does the child need to know?

A song everyone knows by heart, a room where voices can be loud, and hands for conducting waves. Assign parts only after the unison feels solid.

Why this matters

Choir builds breath control, pitch matching and the social skill of blending — being heard AND hearing. Group singing also synchronizes breathing and heartbeats, which is the science behind why choirs feel so good.

What it teaches

Pitch accuracy, breath management, part independence (holding one line among many), ensemble listening, and performance courage shared across the group.

Words to learn

unisonroundpartharmonyblendchorusbreathconductorensemble

Say this to your child

“"Choir club, everyone in! Breathe with me — four in, four out, hisssss. Now all together... and now the MAGIC: you start, and when you reach the mountain, WE start the song over. Listen to us weave!"”

Step by step

  1. Breathing first: four counts in through the nose, four out with a hiss — three rounds, everyone together.
  2. Unison song: the whole family sings one familiar song straight through.
  3. The round: half the family starts, the other half joins two lines later — Row Your Boat is the classic; the weaving is the wow.
  4. Two-part play: half sings a steady oooh drone, half sings the melody above it — swap roles and listen to both.
  5. The concert: one song, both parts, one bow — family choirs deserve audiences and audiences deserve family choirs.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the singer holds the songbook open at singing distance and the mouth is mid-vowel — choirs read and listen simultaneously, which is why the book sits low and the ears stay in charge.

Ask your child

"What did the round sound like?" (the same song chasing itself) "What was your job in the drone part?" (steady and soft) "What makes a choir different from solo singing?" (listening while singing)

What your child can say or do

Your child may conduct the family with full authority, assign the pet a part, or start rounds at dinner without warning — choirs infiltrate households.

Out in the real world

Choirs, a cappella groups, gospel ensembles and every national anthem sung in a stadium run on this training. Professional singers still warm up with the same hiss-breath.

Try it together

Conductor game: one player waves big hands (louder), small hands (softer), a fist (stop) while the choir sings — the conductor swaps every verse, and control of volume becomes a game.

Understanding check

Ask: "What comes first, breathing or singing?" (breathing) "What is a round?" (the same song started late) "What do we do while another part sings?" (listen and hold our line)

This lesson pairs with the Choir flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.
